title: O my body
hookLine: the Guru speaks to the body: what have you done since you came into the world (Anand, the body pauris)

lines: A MAN ON THE STAIRS: COME ON, KNEE.
WE ALL TALK TO OUR BODIES.
THE ANAND DOES IT ON PURPOSE.
cards: Halfway up a long flight of stairs, a man stops, puts a hand on his knee, and says out loud: come on, you can do this. People talk to their bodies all the time.
They scold a stiff back, plead with a stomach before a big meeting, thank their legs at the end of a race. Usually it's a joke, or a complaint.
Near the end of the Anand, Guru Amar Das does it too, on purpose, and his question is not a joke.

teach.h: AE SAREERAA MAIRIAA: O MY BODY.
teach.b: Toward the close of the Anand comes a run of pauris that speak directly to parts of a person. The first begins ae sareeraa mairiaa: O my body.

teach.h: WHAT HAVE YOU DONE SINCE YOU CAME?
teach.b: Then a question, in paraphrase: since you came into this world, what deeds have you done? It sounds like an accusation, and partly it is. The pauri goes on: the One who fashioned you, you never kept in your mind.

teach.h: BY GRACE, THE BODY IS ACCEPTED.
teach.b: By the Guru's grace, the Lord comes to dwell in the mind, and Guru Amar Das ends with a promise: the body that fixes its attention on the True Guru is accepted, approved, parvaan. So the question isn't a verdict.

It's a mirror held up halfway through a life, with a way forward written underneath. And notice who is asked: not the soul, not the mind, the body. This pauri doesn't treat the body as a cage to escape.
Elsewhere Guru Amar Das calls the body the Lord's temple, and Sikh life is lived in the body, as a householder: working, cooking, raising children, serving in langar with your own two hands.
Uncut hair, kept as part of the Khalsa discipline, is explained by some as keeping the body as it was given. The body isn't the problem here.

teach.h: NOT A CAGE: THE ONE BEING INVITED.

teach.b: Hands, feet, a whole lifetime of days: what will they be used for?

how: These pauris are part of the full forty-pauri Anand Sahib, which many Sikhs recite each morning; the Sikh householder way lives faith out in the body, through work, family and service such as langar.

o: the soul, asked where it will go
the body, asked what it has done
the mind, told to stay with the Lord

games.q: the body pauri — tap the pairs.
p: what have you done since you came?
attention fixed on the True Guru

s: the Anand treats the body as a prison to escape
the body is the one invited; Guru Amar Das elsewhere calls it the Lord's temple.
Guru Amar Das speaks directly to the body in the Anand
the pauri opens ae sareeraa mairiaa: O my body.
the body pauri ends in a verdict with no way forward
it ends with a promise: the body turned to the True Guru is accepted.

games.q: the pauri asks the body: what have you done since you came into the world? how does it end?
o: with grace: the body that turns to the True Guru is accepted.
by telling the body to leave the world behind.
games.why: the question is a mirror, not a sentence: by the Guru's grace the Lord dwells in the mind, and that body is parvaan.

practice: Let your attention move slowly from your feet up to your head, and stop at one part that did something for you today: the hands that made breakfast, the legs that carried you to the bus, the lungs, still going.
Rest there and quietly say thank you, the way you'd thank a friend who helped you move house. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once and let it settle into that place.

wordCard.voice: Sareeraa, O body. Ae sareeraa mairiaa: the Anand asks the body what it has done in this world, and promises that the body turned toward the True Guru is accepted.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sareeraa, O body; the form Guru Amar Das uses when he speaks to the body in the Anand.

carryVoice: Your line: what have you done. The pauri asks it with a promise attached. Day three hundred ninety-four.
